scenes.tts: Where does rain go after it lands on your street? Watch a puddle after a storm and you will see water moving downhill. Some rain soaks into the ground. When the ground is full or hard, the rest runs downhill.
scenes.visual: A sloping street with a question mark at the bottom; drops fall, a few soak into the ground, then the rest run down the slope into a growing puddle.
scenes.narration: Where does rain go after it lands on your street? Watch a puddle after a storm and you will see water moving downhill. Some rain soaks into the ground. When the ground is full or hard, the rest runs downhill.

scenes.tts: In the activity, your child crumples paper into hills and valleys. One low corner is coloured blue and called the bay. The high ground is called a ridge. Rain on one side of a ridge flows one way. Rain on the other side flows the other way.
scenes.visual: A flat line crumples into a hill-and-valley cross-section of the paper; the low right corner turns blue as the bay; the ridge is marked; one drop runs left and one runs right.
scenes.narration: In the activity, your child crumples paper into hills and valleys. One low corner is coloured blue and called the bay. The high ground is called a ridge. Rain on one side of a ridge flows one way. Rain on the other side flows the other way.

scenes.tts: All the land that drains to the same stream, river or bay is called a watershed. A ridge splits one watershed from the next. If water pools in more than one low spot on the paper, each pool is collecting rain from its own small patch of land, and some of those pools never reach the bay.
scenes.visual: Same paper cross-section: green brackets mark the land draining to each low spot, a dashed line at the ridge splits them, and the two pools each collect rain from their own patch of land.
scenes.narration: All the land that drains to the same stream, river or bay is called a watershed. A ridge splits one watershed from the next. If water pools in more than one low spot on the paper, each pool is collecting rain from its own small patch of land, and some of those pools never reach the bay.

scenes.tts: Little streams join bigger streams, and bigger streams join rivers. As water runs across the land, it picks things up. Soil, litter, pet waste and lawn fertilizer can all go along. Much of it can end up downstream. In most places, storm drains carry rain straight to a creek without cleaning it.
scenes.visual: A schematic from above: thin streams join into a river that reaches the bay; four labelled bits ride the water downstream; a storm drain feeds a creek.

scenes.tts: More than half of Virginia drains to the Chesapeake Bay. Most of the rest drains south to the sounds of North Carolina or west toward the Gulf of Mexico. A map of Virginia's watersheds helps you find your town.
scenes.visual: A labelled schematic bar, not to scale: a bit more than half drains to the Chesapeake Bay, the rest drains south to North Carolina's sounds or west toward the Gulf of Mexico; a map chip appears.
scenes.narration: More than half of Virginia drains to the Chesapeake Bay. Most of the rest drains south to the sounds of North Carolina or west toward the Gulf of Mexico. A map of Virginia's watersheds helps you find your town.

scenes.tts: Virginia's grade 4 standard asks children to model a watershed and name the one they live in. It also asks them to explain: we all live downstream. If your home is in the Bay watershed, rain that runs off your yard can reach it. It travels through creeks and rivers. Your child can trace which way rain runs from your yard on a map. For a younger child, one idea is enough: what we put on the land can reach the water. The safety notes are on the page.
scenes.visual: Your yard steps down through creek and river to the Bay along a blue path; the words we all live downstream; a note that the safety notes are on the page.
